source.title: A Novel Deep Learning Approach to Malaria Disease Detection on Two Malaria Datasets

record.file_problem: Full text present; Table 4 is flattened, and some plots have no numeric values in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests optimizer and batch-size effects on held-out image-classification results in a malaria-cell setting.
record.gate_note: No random-label, width-scaling, architecture-comparison, dropout-ablation, sharpness, or memorized-example-removal experiment. Training curves are figure-only; cited results in Table 4 are prior work and are not extracted as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study compares adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out malaria images, bearing on V4. It also provides a fixed-learning-rate batch comparison relevant to V5: Section II.B specifies batch 12 and learning rate 1e-5 for Table 2, while Table 1 reports batch 64 at the same learning rate, with 50 epochs throughout.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors identify Nadam as best by misclassification count, report 95% accuracy for Nadam and RMSprop, and recommend Nadam, RMSprop and Adam for their proposed malaria CNN. They also state that adding the second dataset did not change performance, without reporting optimizer-specific numerical results for that comparison.
record.recipe_differences: Malaria-image classification with a proposed CNN and optimizer comparison; no arbitrary-label memorization or generalization-gap measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer choice changes reported performance. Table 1 varies batch size and learning rate together; optimizer-specific results also vary.

fits_no_version.finding: Ftrl performs poorly, with overall accuracy 0.25 stated in the conclusion, but its classification metrics and error counts are internally inconsistent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice strongly affects malaria-classification performance under a shared training recipe.

record.peer_reviewed: Bilecik Şeyh Edebali Üniversitesi Fen Bilimleri Dergisi / BSEU Journal of Science, 2023, 10(2)
record.problems: No random-label or memorization-capacity check. Training and test accuracy curves are figure-only, so numerical train-test gaps cannot be calculated. Table 1 changes batch size and learning rate together. The second dataset robustness result is stated qualitatively without values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 precision, recall, and F1 values are not separately extracted because the accuracy rows preserve the optimizer test-performance comparison. Table 3 loss counts are omitted as a second presentation of error counts rather than a distinct train-test gap measure. Table 4 cited comparisons are prior work, not this study’s results.

untested.parts: No random-label fitting experiment or comparison with natural-label generalization.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold experiment.
No controlled convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.

No optimizer-specific learning-rate or schedule tuning, broad-tuning comparison, decoupled-weight-decay intervention, optimizer switching, or language benchmark. Training-performance parity is not quantified; the text says training and test rankings are parallel.

No batch-size threshold sweep, longer-training intervention, learning-rate scaling with warmup, or normalization/regularization adaptation. Only batch sizes 12 and 64 have a recoverable matched-learning-rate comparison.
Dropout is used but never ablated or varied.
No weight-perturbation sharpness measurements or comparisons of generalization measures.
No memorization-based example removal or random-removal control.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. The extraction overlooks the matched batch comparison obtainable across Tables 1 and 2. Shared learning rates provide limited evidence about optimizer generalization because they need not suit every optimizer, and the training rankings reportedly track the test rankings. Class-labelled accuracy rows mostly duplicate overall accuracy rather than provide independent outcomes. The schema permits only one state per row: R1–R6 are marked reversed for V4 and serve as baselines for the observed V5 effect. No repeated-run uncertainty or precise train/test split is supplied.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or natural-label generalization comparison.
No CNN versus fully connected comparison.
No language benchmark, broad tuning comparison, weight-decay intervention, or switch from Adam to SGD.
Batch-size comparison does not isolate batch size from learning rate; no large-batch normalization or regularization changes.
Dropout is part of the proposed model but is not ablated.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure analysis.

relationships.condition: Nadam, RMSprop, Adam and Adamax versus SGD; proposed malaria CNN, 50 epochs, batch 12, common learning rate 1e-5
relationships.reason: R1–R10 report adaptive accuracies of 0.92–0.95 versus SGD's 0.86, reversing the expected disadvantage under this shared, minimally tuned recipe.
relationships.display_finding: Nadam, RMSprop, Adam and Adamax reportedly achieved accuracies of 0.92–0.95 versus SGD's 0.86, but these shared-learning-rate comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Adagrad and Adadelta versus SGD under the same malaria-CNN recipe
relationships.reason: R11–R14 report accuracies of 0.69 and 0.56 versus SGD's 0.86 in R9–R10; these adaptive methods perform worse.
relationships.display_finding: Reported accuracy favored SGD over both adaptive methods under the shared recipe, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Batch 64 versus batch 12 with Nadam, RMSprop and Adam; learning rate 1e-5, 50 epochs
relationships.reason: R23–R28 report accuracy 0.88–0.89 at batch 64 versus 0.94–0.95 in R1–R6 at batch 12; Section II.B supplies the matched baseline settings.
relationships.display_finding: The study's comparisons suggest lower accuracy with the larger batch across Nadam, RMSprop and Adam. These comparisons have not been verified.
